nameStory: The name 'clammy goosefoot' comes from two distinctive features of this small plant. The 'clammy' part refers to the sticky, slightly wet feeling of its leaves when you touch them, while 'goosefoot' describes the shape of the leaves, which resemble a goose's webbed foot with their triangular lobes.
description: Clammy goosefoot is a small, weedy annual plant that rarely grows taller than your knee. It's a world traveler from Australia that has made itself at home in disturbed areas throughout New England. The plant has a bushy, spreading growth habit with small triangular leaves and tiny clusters of inconspicuous flowers. What makes it memorable is its distinctly sticky texture and its tendency to pop up in parking lots, roadsides, and other disturbed ground.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small triangular leaves that feel noticeably sticky or clammy to the touch, with a slightly wet sensation even when dry weather

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing, bushy annual that spreads outward more than upward, typically staying under 2 feet tall with multiple branching stems

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, greenish flowers clustered in small groups along the stems, easily overlooked and lacking petals

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Overall plant feels glandular and sticky when brushed against, leaving a slight residue on clothing or skin

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark seeds that develop in tiny papery capsules after the inconspicuous flowers fade

habitat: Look for clammy goosefoot in disturbed areas like parking lots, roadsides, waste ground, and construction sites throughout New England. It thrives in compacted soils and sunny locations where other plants struggle to establish. You'll often find it growing alongside other weedy species in urban and suburban environments.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and begin their low, spreading growth pattern. The characteristic sticky leaves are already noticeable on small seedlings.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with full leaf development and inconspicuous flowering. The clammy texture is most pronounced during warm, humid weather.
seasonality.fall: Plants continue flowering and producing seeds until first frost. Seeds mature and scatter for next year's generation.
seasonality.winter: Annual plant dies back completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to sprout the following spring.

funFact: This little plant is thought to have hitchhiked from Australia to Europe hidden in wool shipments, earning it passage around the world by clinging to sheep's fleece with its sticky leaves - nature's own version of velcro!
confusionNotes: Other small goosefoot family members can look similar, but the distinctly clammy, sticky feel of the leaves sets this species apart from its relatives. When in doubt, give it the 'touch test' - if it feels noticeably sticky or glandular, you've likely found clammy goosefoot.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'goosefoot,' this plant was recently moved from the traditional goosefoot family (Chenopodiaceae) into the amaranth family (Amaranthaceae) based on genetic studies, though it still shares the characteristic triangular leaf shape that gives goosefoots their name.
compareHints: Compared to its relatives like Mexican tea and Jerusalem oak, clammy goosefoot is much smaller and has the distinctive sticky texture. Mexican tea has a strong, medicinal smell when crushed, while Jerusalem oak has more deeply lobed leaves that look almost oak-like. Clammy goosefoot's simple triangular leaves and glandular stickiness make it unique among its genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Mexican tea differs from its relatives like clammy goosefoot and Jerusalem oak primarily by its much stronger, more pungent smell and its narrow, lance-shaped leaves.

Unlike its Dysphania relatives like Mexican tea (which has a strong, pungent odor when crushed) or clammy goosefoot (which feels sticky), winged pigweed is distinguished by its papery stem wings and lack of strong scent.
Jerusalem oak stands out from its Dysphania relatives by its deeply cut, almost fern-like leaves - Mexican tea and clammy goosefoot have much simpler, less divided leaves.
